units.subject: math
units.title: Addition and Subtraction Within 10
units.metaTitle: Grade 1 Math Lesson Plans: Addition and Subtraction Within 10
units.metaDescription: A five-week Grade 1 math unit: 8 lessons on adding and subtracting within 10, each with a teacher note, practice pages (most at three levels), and on-screen practice.

lessons.title: Add two groups
lessons.objective: Children join two groups with a total of up to 10, count how many there are altogether, and write the total as a number.

screen.title: Domino Math

note.mistake: Many children count the first group, start again at 1 for the second group, and write that second number as the total. Others count one picture twice or skip one.
note.words: Ask: "How many in this group? How many in that group? How many altogether?" Point to the plus sign and the equal sign and say "plus" and "equals"; tell the children that "equals" means "is the same as." Use "altogether" and "in all" for the total.
note.watch: Watch who touches each picture once while counting. A child who says the first number and counts on from it ("four… five, six") is ready for the harder page.

lessons.title: Take away: how many are left?
lessons.objective: Children look at a group of up to 10 pictures with some crossed out, count how many are left, and write that number.

screen.title: Show the Operation — Add & Subtract on a Ten Frame

note.mistake: Children count the crossed-out pictures instead of the ones left, or count every picture, crossed out or not, and write the number they started with.
note.words: Say: "Start with six. Take away two. How many are left?" Read 6 − 2 as "six take away two" first, then as "six minus two."
note.watch: Ask each child to point to the pictures that are left before writing the answer. A child who is unsure can act it out first: lay out six counters, slide two away, and count the ones that stay.

lessons.title: Partners that make 10
lessons.objective: Children find the number that goes with a given number to make 10, and know the pairs that make 10.

paper.title: Addition Maze for 1st Grade: Sums That Make 10

screen.title: Make 10 — Number Bonds to Ten

note.mistake: Children know 5 + 5 and 9 + 1 but count from 1 for the other pairs. Many do not see that 3 + 7 and 7 + 3 are the same pair.
note.words: Ask: "What goes with 6 to make 10?" Call the two numbers "partners of 10." On a ten frame: "Six are full. How many are empty?"
note.watch: Who answers from the empty spaces without counting the full ones again? Those children can go on to the maze; the others stay with the ten frame.

lessons.title: Count on and count back on a number line
lessons.objective: Children add by hopping forward and subtract by hopping back on a number line, starting from the first number.

screen.title: Hopper's Number Line — Add & Subtract by Hopping

note.mistake: Children count the starting number as the first hop, so 5 + 3 lands on 7. Counting back, they land one too high for the same reason.
note.words: Say: "Put your finger on 5 and say five. Now hop three times and count as you land: six, seven, eight." Use "hop forward" for adding and "hop back" for subtracting.
note.watch: Watch the first hop. A child who says the starting number while moving lands one short. Have the child draw each hop as an arc and count the arcs, not the marks: three arcs for + 3.

lessons.title: Fact families to 10
lessons.objective: Children use three related numbers to write the two addition facts and the two subtraction facts that belong together.

screen.title: Find the Missing Part — Subtraction as a Number Bond

note.mistake: Children write 3 + 7 = 10 and 7 + 3 = 10 easily, then write 3 − 7 = 10 or 7 − 10 = 3, because they move the numbers around without thinking about which one is the whole.
note.words: Ask: "Which number is the whole? Which two are the parts?" Then: "The parts add up to the whole. The whole take away one part leaves the other part."
note.watch: Check that each subtraction fact starts from the whole. If it does not, go back to the three numbers on a number bond, cover one part, and ask what is left.

lessons.title: Find the missing number
lessons.objective: Children find the unknown number in an addition or subtraction equation within 10, in any position.

screen.title: Fixit's Fix-It Corner — Find the Missing Number

note.mistake: Children add the two numbers they can see: for 4 + □ = 9 they write 13. For □ − 3 = 5 many write 2.
note.words: Read the box as "what number": "Four plus what number makes nine?" Read the equal sign as "is the same as."
note.watch: Have the child read the finished equation aloud and say whether it is true. A child who counts up from 4 to 9 on fingers has understood the idea.

lessons.title: Word problems within 10
lessons.objective: Children solve addition and subtraction story problems within 10 and say or write the equation that tells the story.

screen.title: Vet's Diagnosis Window — Word-Problem Modeling

note.mistake: Children pick out the two numbers and add them no matter what the story says, or look for one word such as "more" and choose the operation from it.
note.words: Ask: "What happens in the story? Are things joining or leaving?" Have the child retell the story before any number is written. Then: "Write the equation that tells the story." The page has a box for the answer only, so have the children write the equation next to the picture.
note.watch: Listen to the retelling. A child who can act the story out with counters but writes the wrong sign needs the link from the action to the sign, not more counting.

lessons.title: Fact fluency within 10
lessons.objective: Children add and subtract within 10 without counting every time, using facts they know and facts they can figure out.

screen.title: Mental Math to 10

note.mistake: Children count every fact from 1, even 5 + 1 or 4 + 4, because counting has always given them the right answer. When they are pushed to be fast, they stop counting and guess.
note.words: Ask: "Which facts do you just know? Which ones can you figure out from a fact you know?" For example: "I know 4 + 4, so 4 + 5 is one more."
note.watch: Note which facts each child still counts for. A child who counts most of them gets the easier page for more practice; write the facts on the class record so you know what to come back to. Do not time this page.

units.subject: literacy
units.title: Hearing Sounds in Words
units.metaTitle: Kindergarten Reading and Writing Lesson Plans: Hearing Sounds in Words
units.metaDescription: A three-week Kindergarten unit: 6 lessons from rhyme and syllables to sound boxes and first CVC words. The last two are for children who know most letter sounds.

lessons.title: Hear the rhyme
lessons.objective: Children say two picture words aloud and decide whether they rhyme.

screen.title: Rosa Raccoon's Rhyme Wagon — Hear & Match Rhymes

note.mistake: Children match words that begin with the same sound (cat, cup) or that go together in meaning (cat, dog) instead of words that sound the same at the end.
note.words: Say: "Rhyming words sound the same at the end. Cat, hat: -at, -at." Say the pair, then stretch the ending.
note.watch: Name every picture together before the children start; a child who calls a picture by another name cannot find its rhyme. Have each child say both words aloud before marking.

lessons.title: Clap the syllables
lessons.objective: Children say a word and count its syllables by clapping the beats.

screen.title: Build Words from Syllables — Phonics

note.mistake: Children clap once for each sound (three claps for "cat"), or stretch the word and add beats that are not there.
note.words: Say: "Syllables are the beats in a word. Say it the way you talk and clap the beats: ti-ger. Two." A hand under the chin works too: the chin drops once for each beat.
note.watch: One-beat words are the test: who claps "dog" once? Ask children who stretch the word to say it at talking speed.

lessons.title: Beginning sounds
lessons.objective: Children say a picture word, hear its first sound, and match it to the letter.

screen.title: Beginning Sounds — Match the First Letter Sound

note.mistake: Children say the letter name instead of the sound, or give the whole first syllable ("ba" for banana).
note.words: Ask: "What is the very first sound your mouth makes? Mmm… moon." Say the sound without adding "uh": hold /m/ as "mmm," not "muh"; make /b/ quick and quiet, not "buh."
note.watch: Ask: "Say it. What sound did you start with?" A child who can say the sound but not find the letter needs letter practice, not more listening.

lessons.title: Ending sounds and middle sounds
lessons.objective: Children say a picture word, listen for its last sound or for the vowel in the middle, and write the letter for that sound.

screen.title: Coco's Sound Boxes — First, Middle & Last Sounds

note.mistake: Children who have just learned to listen for the first sound keep answering with it. The middle vowel is the hardest part: short e and short i are mixed up most.
note.words: Say: "Say the word. What is the last sound you hear? Bus… /s/." For the middle: "Stretch it: sss-uuu-nnn. What is in the middle?"
note.watch: A child who writes the first letter for every picture has not moved to the end of the word yet. Go back to saying the word together and catching its last sound. Give ending sounds and middle sounds a day each.

lessons.title: Say it slowly: one sound, one box
lessons.objective: Children say a word slowly, count its sounds, and put one sound in each box.

screen.title: Count the Sounds

note.mistake: Children give the beats from the syllable lesson instead of the sounds, so "ship" gets one dot. Others break the word into two parts only, /sh/ and "ip," and run the last two sounds together in one box. Children who already know how a word is spelled may count its letters: four dots for "ship."
note.words: Warm up by blending. Say the sounds of a word one at a time, /s/ /u/ /n/, and ask: "What word?" Do five words before the children open the page. Then say: "Touch a box for each sound: /sh/ /i/ /p/. Three sounds." On the Count the Sounds page say "sound," never "letter." On the Sound Boxes page say: "Now write the letter or letters for each sound. Sh is two letters and one sound, so both go in the wide box."
note.watch: Watch the fingers, not the paper: one touch for each sound. Words with two letters for one sound show who is counting sounds and who is spelling; keep those words for the children who are ready for the harder page.

lessons.title: Build the word
lessons.objective: Children build a three-sound word for a picture from its letters, in the order of its sounds.

screen.title: Build the CVC Word — Phonics

note.mistake: Children write the first and last sound and leave out the vowel ("ct" for cat), or put the letters in the wrong order ("cta").
note.words: Ask: "Say the word. First sound? Next sound? Last sound?" After writing: "Touch and say each sound, then read the whole word."
note.watch: Have each child read back what they built. A child who reads "ct" as "cat" is reading from the picture; cover the picture and ask again.

units.subject: math
units.title: Position Words, Size, and Patterns
units.metaTitle: Kindergarten Math Lesson Plans: Position Words, Size, and Patterns
units.metaDescription: A three-week Kindergarten math unit: 5 lessons on position words, searching a picture, comparing sizes, and repeating patterns, each with a teacher note.

lessons.title: Position words
lessons.objective: Children use the words on, under, beside, left, and right to say where something is, and circle the picture in the place that is named.

screen.title: Bramble's Parking Tower — Position Words: Above, Below, Between

note.mistake: Children circle the picture they like best, not the one in the place that was named. Left and right are the hardest: many children find the correct side only while they face the same way as the teacher.
note.words: Say the whole sentence each time: "The cat is ON the box. The ball is UNDER the box." For left and right, stand with your back to the children so that your left is their left, and say: "Put your finger on the line. Slide it this way. This is the LEFT side." Have children say the position word back to you.
note.watch: Watch who can also SAY where a picture is, not only circle it. A child who mixes up left and right but knows on, under, and beside needs more turns with the line page, not with the box page.

lessons.title: Find every one like it
lessons.objective: Children search a busy picture for every picture or shape like the one in the box and circle them all.

note.mistake: Children circle the first two or three they see and stop, or they circle a picture that is only the same color or nearly the same shape.
note.words: Ask: "Is it exactly like the one in the box? Did you find them all? How do you know?" Teach a path for the eyes: "Start at the top and go row by row, like reading."
note.watch: Watch who searches in order and who jumps around the page. Children who jump around miss pictures; give them a strip of paper to slide down the page row by row.

lessons.title: Biggest and tallest
lessons.objective: Children compare the pictures in a row and circle the biggest or the tallest one.

screen.title: Comparing Length — Taller, Shorter, Longer | Measurement

note.mistake: Children say "big" for everything: a tall thing and a long thing are both "the big one." Some circle the picture that sits highest on the page and not the tallest one.
note.words: Use a different word for each kind of size: "We say TALL for things that stand up, like a tree. We say BIG for the one that takes up the most room." Ask: "Do they all stand on the same line? Look from the bottom to the top. Which one is the TALLEST?" Ask for the opposite too: "Which one is the shortest?"
note.watch: Watch who looks at every picture in the row before circling. A child who circles after looking at only two should touch each picture first and say its size word.

lessons.title: Put them in order by size
lessons.objective: Children put three or five pictures in order from smallest to biggest and number them, starting with 1 for the smallest.

screen.title: The Faraway Shelf — Compare Lengths with a Cord

note.mistake: With three pictures children find the smallest and the biggest and guess the middle one. With five they get the two ends and mix up the middle, or they number the pictures from left to right without looking at the sizes.
note.words: Say: "Find the smallest. That one is number 1. Now look at the ones that are left. Which is the smallest NOW?" Use "smaller than" and "bigger than": "The cup is bigger than the spoon and smaller than the pot."
note.watch: Watch who starts over with "the smallest of what is left" each time. That child has a method and can do five pictures; a child who guesses should stay with three.

lessons.title: What comes next?
lessons.objective: Children read a repeating pattern aloud, find the part that repeats, and circle what comes next.

note.mistake: Children look only at the last picture and choose one that is different from it. That works for a two-part pattern and fails for a three-part one. Others copy the first picture of the row every time.
note.words: Read the pattern aloud together and tap it: "apple, pear, apple, pear, apple…" Stop and let the class say the next one. Ask: "Which part keeps coming back?" Call it "the part that repeats."
note.watch: Watch who can tell you the part that repeats ("apple, pear"), not only the next picture. A child who chants the row correctly and circles the wrong picture stopped chanting before looking at the choices: have the child chant the row again, say the next word aloud, and only then look for it among the choices.

units.subject: math
units.title: Counting to 10
units.metaTitle: Kindergarten Math Lesson Plans: Counting to 10
units.metaDescription: A three-week Kindergarten math unit: 7 lessons on matching one to one, writing numbers, counting to 10, quick looks, and comparing groups, each with a teacher note.

lessons.title: One for each
lessons.objective: Children give each object exactly one partner by drawing a line, and say whether there are enough.

screen.title: Twinsies — Count How Many & Count Out That Many

note.mistake: Children draw two lines to the same partner, or skip one that sits a little off to the side. When one is left without a partner, they draw a line to a picture that already has one so that nobody is left out.
note.words: Say: "One for you, one for you. Each one gets ONE partner." When something is left over: "Is there one for each? Which group has more?" Use "enough" and "not enough."
note.watch: Watch the lines: one line from each picture and one line to each picture. A child who gives one picture two lines should put a finger on each partner as it is used ("this one is taken"). A child who can tell you "there are not enough" without counting understands matching.

lessons.title: Write the numbers 0 to 9
lessons.objective: Children trace and write the numbers 0 to 9, starting each one at the dot and following the arrows.

screen.title: Digby's Number Trace — Write Every Number 0 to 9

note.mistake: Children start at the bottom and draw the number like a picture, so 8 comes out as two circles stacked up and 9 as a ball with a stick added. Reversed 2, 3, 5, and 7 are common at this age and are not a sign of a problem.
note.words: Give every number a short saying and use the same one all year, for example for 5: "Down, around, then put on its hat." Ask: "Where does it start? At the orange dot. Which way does the arrow go?"
note.watch: Watch the hand, not the finished page: a number that looks right can be written from the bottom up. Check the pencil grip while children trace, and correct one number at a time.

lessons.title: Count and write how many
lessons.objective: Children count up to 10 pictures, say the last number as how many there are, and write that number.

screen.title: How Many Animals? Count 1 to 10 — Ten Frame Activity

note.mistake: Children say the numbers faster than they touch, so they count a picture twice or skip one. Asked "How many?" after counting, some start counting again and do not say the last number.
note.words: Say: "Touch one, say one number." After the count ask: "So how many are there?" and wait for one number, not a recount. On the ten frame: "The top row is full. That is five. Six, seven."
note.watch: Watch the finger and the voice together. A child whose voice runs ahead of the finger should cross out each picture while saying its number. A backward 3 or 7 in the written answer is a handwriting matter, not a counting mistake.

lessons.title: Make a group of that many
lessons.objective: Children read a number and color or draw exactly that many, stopping when they reach the number.

screen.title: Count to 10 with Animals — Ten Frame Activity

note.mistake: Children color all the pictures in the row. They can count a group that is already there, but they do not stop when they reach the number they were given.
note.words: Say: "The number says 4. Color one, two, three, four. STOP. Is that four? Check." Have the child say the number before starting and again at the end: "I need four. I have four."
note.watch: Watch who stops alone at the number and who needs your "stop." A child who needs it should keep the number in sight: one finger on the number while the other hand colors.

lessons.title: Color by number
lessons.objective: Children read the number in each part of a picture and color the part with the color the key gives for that number.

paper.title: Color by Number: Shapes with a Code

screen.title: Color by Number: Picture Scenes

note.mistake: Children color by what the thing should look like ("grass is green") and not by the number. They mix up 6 and 9, or color a part next door because they did not look inside it for its number.
note.words: Say: "Find the number inside the part. Find that number in the key. What color does the key say?" Do one color at a time: "Find every 3 first. All the 3s are blue."
note.watch: Watch who goes back to the key for each part. One color at a time keeps the key in mind and shows you quickly who cannot yet tell 6 from 9.

lessons.title: How many? Look fast
lessons.objective: Children look at a small group for a moment and say how many there are without counting one by one.

screen.title: How Many Are There? — Counting

note.mistake: Children count every dot with a finger even for two or three. In five or six dots they do not see the smaller groups (a four and a two), so they have nothing to do but count.
note.words: Show a group for two seconds, cover it, and ask: "How many did you see? HOW did you see them?" Accept "I saw two and two." Say: "You did not count. Your eyes knew."
note.watch: Watch for moving lips and pointing fingers: those children are still counting by ones. Stay with one to four for them and use dice patterns, which look the same every time.

lessons.title: More and fewer
lessons.objective: Children compare two groups and tell which has more and which has fewer.

screen.title: Which Group Has More? — Counting

note.mistake: Children choose the group that takes up more room or has the bigger pictures, not the one with more in it. "Fewer" is a new word for most children; on that page they circle the bigger group again.
note.words: Ask: "Which group has MORE? How can we check?" Check by matching one to one or by counting both. Say "fewer" for things and "less than" for numbers: "There are fewer cats than dogs. Five is more than three. Three is less than five." Show two equal groups once: "These two groups have the same number."
note.watch: Watch what children do when the smaller group is spread out wide. A child who counts or matches before answering is ready; a child who answers at a glance and is wrong should line the two groups up.

units.subject: math
units.title: Shapes All Around
units.metaTitle: Kindergarten Math Lesson Plans: Shapes All Around
units.metaDescription: A two-week Kindergarten math unit: 4 lessons on naming shapes, counting sides, building with tangram pieces, and mirror pictures, each with a teacher note.

lessons.title: Name the shape
lessons.objective: Children name circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles, even when a shape is turned, long, or thin.

screen.title: Professor Pip's Museum — Name Shapes Any Way They Turn

note.mistake: Children know a triangle only when it sits flat with the point on top. A triangle standing on its point is "upside down" or "not a triangle," and a square on its corner becomes "a diamond."
note.words: Turn a shape in your hand and ask: "Is it still a triangle? Why?" Give the reason every time: "It has three straight sides and three corners, so it is a triangle." For the turned square: "Four sides all the same length and four square corners. It is still a square."
note.watch: Listen to what children say about the long, thin triangle and the turned square. A child who counts the sides to decide is using the rule; a child who says "it does not look like one" is going by the picture.

lessons.title: Count the sides
lessons.objective: Children count the sides of a shape, write the number, and match shapes to their number of sides.

screen.title: Count the Sides — Geometry

note.mistake: Children count around the shape and forget where they started, so one side is counted twice. Some count sides and corners together, and some say a circle has one side.
note.words: Say: "Put a mark on the side where you start. Trace each side with your finger and count. Stop at your mark." Ask: "Is a side straight? Then how many straight sides does a circle have?" (None.)
note.watch: Watch who marks a starting side. Check the six-sided shapes first: that is where a double count shows.

lessons.title: Build shapes from pieces
lessons.objective: Children put tangram pieces together to make a figure and show where the pieces meet inside a shape.

paper.title: Easy Tangram Puzzles: Draw the Lines for 2 and 3 Pieces
Tangram Puzzles: Cut Out the Pieces and Build Two Figures

screen.title: Mim's Glow Workshop — Compose Shapes from Pattern Blocks

note.mistake: Children lay a piece down the way it came off the page and give up when it does not fit. They do not think of turning it or flipping it over. On the drawing page they draw a line where no two pieces could meet.
note.words: Say: "Turn it. Flip it. Slide it." Name what happened: "Two small triangles made a square." Ask: "Which piece fills this corner? Which side of the piece is the long side?"
note.watch: Watch who turns a piece before asking for help. Scissors are part of this lesson: a child who cuts off a corner cannot make the pieces fit, so cut the sets ahead of time for children who are still learning to cut on a line.

lessons.title: Mirror pictures
lessons.objective: Children look at a picture and choose the one that shows it the way a mirror would.

note.mistake: Children circle the picture that is exactly the same, or the one that is upside down. They do not yet see that a mirror swaps left and right and keeps top and bottom.
note.words: Hold a small mirror beside a picture and ask: "The dog looks left. Which way does the dog in the mirror look?" Say: "In a mirror, left and right trade places. Up stays up."
note.watch: Notice which wrong answer a child picks. The same picture means the child has not seen the swap; the upside-down picture means the child is turning, not flipping. Show the difference: draw a dog with a thick marker on one half of a folded sheet, hold it against the window and trace it on the other half, then open the sheet. The two dogs face each other, and neither one is upside down.

units.subject: math
units.title: Counting in Order to 20
units.metaTitle: Kindergarten Math Lesson Plans: Counting in Order to 20
units.metaDescription: A two-week Kindergarten math unit: 4 lessons on counting forward to 20, connecting dots in order, counting back from 10, and first, second, third.

lessons.title: Fill in the missing numbers
lessons.objective: Children count along a number strip to 10 and to 20 and write the numbers that are missing.

screen.title: What Number Comes Next? — Counting

note.mistake: Children can count from 1 but cannot say what comes after a number in the middle. To fill a gap after 7 they go back and whisper from 1. In the teens they say "three-teen" and "five-teen," skip 13 or 15, or write the digits in the order they hear them: 31 for thirteen, 71 for seventeen.
note.words: Ask: "What comes right after 7? Say it without starting at 1." Count on together from different numbers: "Start at 6. Seven, eight, nine." Say the teen numbers slowly and point: "thir-teen, four-teen, fif-teen."
note.watch: Watch who whispers from 1 for every gap. That child needs many short "start at… and count on" turns aloud before more pages. Check 11, 12, 13, and 15, the numbers that do not sound like what they are.

lessons.title: Connect the dots in order
lessons.objective: Children connect numbered dots in counting order, from 1 to 10 and from 11 to 20, to finish a picture.

screen.title: Count the Stars Awake — Counting On from a Number

note.mistake: Children connect a dot to the nearest dot, not to the next number. They read 12 as 21, or they lift the pencil, lose their place, and cannot find where they were.
note.words: Say: "Say the number you are on. What comes next? Find it BEFORE you draw." Keep one finger on the dot you are on and look for the next number with your eyes.
note.watch: Watch the first three lines. A child who looks for the next number before moving the pencil will finish alone. If the picture comes out wrong, count aloud along the lines together to find where it left the order.

lessons.title: Before, after, and counting back
lessons.objective: Children write the number that comes before and the number that comes after, and count backward from 10.

screen.title: Before and After

note.mistake: "After" is easy because it is the next counting word. "Before" is hard: children write the number after again, or count up from 1 to find it. Counting back, they skip a number or jump from 10 to 8.
note.words: On a number line: "Put your finger on 6. The number BEFORE is one step back. The number AFTER is one step forward." Count down like a rocket: "10, 9, 8…" Say "one less" for before and "one more" for after.
note.watch: Watch who finds the number before without counting up from 1. Children who cannot should use the number line for every item; take it away only when they stop looking at it.

lessons.title: First, second, third
lessons.objective: Children find the first, second, third, and later places in a line, counting from the end that is marked.

screen.title: Ordinal Numbers: Find the Place

note.mistake: Children always count from the left, even when the arrow or the flag is on the right. Some mark that many pictures (three pictures for "third") and not the one picture in third place.
note.words: Ask first: "Where does the line start? Find the arrow." Then: "First, second, third. The THIRD one is only this one." Line up five children and ask: "Who is second? Now turn around. Who is second now?"
note.watch: Watch what happens when the start is on the right. A child who looks for the arrow before counting has the idea. Keep "three" and "third" apart: "Three is how many. Third is which one."

units.subject: math
units.title: Sorting, Tallies, and the Days of the Week
units.metaTitle: Kindergarten Math Lesson Plans: Sorting, Tallies, and Days of the Week
units.metaDescription: A three-week Kindergarten math unit: 5 lessons on counting each kind, tally marks, estimating, heavier and lighter, and the days of the week, with teacher notes.

lessons.title: Count each kind
lessons.objective: Children look at a mixed group of pictures, count each kind separately, and write how many of each there are.

screen.title: Sort and Count — Classify Objects by Category | Measurement & Data

note.mistake: Children count everything on the page as one group, or they count one kind and lose track because the pictures are mixed. A picture gets counted twice or not at all.
note.words: Say: "We are counting only the birds now. Is this a bird? Then mark it." Teach children to cross out or dot each picture as they count it. Ask afterward: "Which kind has the most?"
note.watch: Watch who marks what has been counted. A child who marks and still gets a wrong number has a counting problem: count aloud together, touching each mark. A child who does not mark has a keeping-track problem: hand that child a crayon and have every counted picture crossed out.

lessons.title: Tally marks
lessons.objective: Children show a count with tally marks, crossing the fifth mark over the first four, and read a tally back as a number.

note.mistake: Children draw five upright marks and cross them with a sixth, so every bundle is worth six. Others never cross and draw one long row of single marks.
note.words: Chant while drawing: "One, two, three, four, and SHUT THE GATE." Say: "The gate is number five. It is not an extra one." To read a tally, start from the bundle: "Five… six, seven." With two bundles: "Five, ten… eleven."
note.watch: Watch children draw: count the upright marks before the cross goes on. When they read a tally, listen for "five" said at once for a bundle and not "one, two, three, four, five."

lessons.title: Take a good guess
lessons.objective: Children look at a group, choose the better guess for how many there are, and then check by counting.

screen.title: The Wondering Jar — Guess, Then Count to Find Out

note.mistake: Children count quietly before they guess, because they want to be right. Or they give a wild number ("a hundred") for eight things. Both show that a guess is not yet a thinking step for them.
note.words: Say: "A good guess has a math name: an ESTIMATE. An estimate is not a count. Look, think, and tell me: closer to 5 or closer to 20?" After the count: "Was your estimate close? It does not have to be the same." Praise close estimates, not only exact ones.
note.watch: Watch who changes the circled guess after counting. Tell the class that a guess stays as it was; the count is a second answer. Notice who uses a group they know ("that looks like a full ten frame").

lessons.title: Which is heavier?
lessons.objective: Children look at two everyday objects and circle the one that is heavier.

screen.title: Heavy or Light?

note.mistake: Children circle the thing that looks bigger. A big balloon is chosen over a small rock, because to them bigger has always meant more.
note.words: Bring a balloon and a rock, or a big empty box and a small full bottle: "Which is bigger? Which is heavier? Hold one in each hand." Say: "Big is how much room it takes up. Heavy is how hard it pushes down on your hand."
note.watch: Look at the pairs where the smaller thing is the heavier one; those tell you who understands. Let children be the balance: arms out, one thing in each hand, and the heavy side goes down. If two things feel about the same, put them on a pan balance.

lessons.title: The days of the week
lessons.objective: Children say the seven days of the week in order and put the days in order on a page.

paper.title: Days of the Week in Order
Missing Days: Write the Week in Order

screen.title: Missing Days: Write the Week in Order

exit.title: Days of the Week in Order

note.mistake: Children can sing the days in order but cannot start in the middle: asked what comes after Wednesday, they sing from the beginning. Tuesday and Thursday get mixed up because they start alike.
note.words: Ask every morning: "What day is it today? What day was yesterday? What day will it be tomorrow?" Point to the words while the class says them. For the two T days, look at the second letter: "Tuesday starts with T-U. Thursday starts with T-H, like 'three.'"
note.watch: Watch who has to start the whole song for each answer. On the copying page, check that each word is copied letter by letter from the word bank; that page is reading and writing as much as math.

units.subject: math
units.title: Putting Together and Number Bonds
units.metaTitle: Kindergarten Math Lesson Plans: Putting Together and Number Bonds
units.metaDescription: A three-week Kindergarten math unit: 5 lessons on putting groups together and number bonds to 5 and to 10, with a first look at partners that make 20 and at odd and even.

lessons.title: How many altogether?
lessons.objective: Children put two groups together, count all of them, and write how many there are in all.

screen.title: Show the Operation — Add & Subtract on a Ten Frame

note.mistake: Children count the first group, then start again at 1 for the second group and write that second number. They count two groups; they do not yet join them.
note.words: Say: "Here are three. Here are two. Push them together. How many ALTOGETHER?" Count across the gap without stopping: "one, two, three… four, five." Then say and write the sentence: "Three and two make five. Three plus two equals five: 3 + 2 = 5." Use "altogether" and "in all" for the total.
note.watch: Watch what happens at the gap between the groups. A child who keeps counting has joined them. A child who says the first number and counts on from it is already using a first-grade strategy; let it be.

lessons.title: Number bonds to 5 and to 10
lessons.objective: Children break a number up to 10 into two parts and find the part that is missing in a number bond.

screen.title: Make 10 — Number Bonds to Ten

note.mistake: Children add the two numbers they see. When the bond shows 5 on top and 2 below, they write 7 in the empty circle, because every number so far was something to add.
note.words: Point and say: "The top circle is the WHOLE. The two circles below are the PARTS." Ask: "Five is the whole. Two is one part. What is the other part?" Show it with five counters: "Two here. How many are over there?"
note.watch: Look for answers bigger than the whole: that child added. Go back to counters and split one group in different ways before returning to the page.

lessons.title: Add and subtract to color
lessons.objective: Children solve addition and subtraction facts and color each part of a picture with the color for its answer.

screen.title: Quick Facts to 5 — Add & Subtract Fluently

note.mistake: Children see two numbers and add, even when the sign is a minus. Or they solve the fact correctly and then color by the first number in the problem and not by the answer.
note.words: Say: "Circle the sign first. Is it plus or minus?" Then: "Write the answer small in the part. Now look in the code for THAT number." Let children use fingers or a ten frame; this page is practice, not a speed test.
note.watch: Watch who writes the answers before coloring. The picture shows mistakes by itself: a part in the wrong color is a fact to check together. The easier pages stay within 5, where Kindergarten children are expected to be fluent; the standard pages go to 10, so keep counters or a ten frame at hand.

lessons.title: Partners that make 20
lessons.objective: Children find the number that goes with a given number to make 20, using the partners that make 10.

screen.title: Find the Total — Add Two Parts Within 20

note.mistake: Children who know the partners of 10 do not use them here: for 13 and what make 20 they count up by ones from 13 and are often off by one. They do not see that 13 is 10 and 3, so its partner is the partner of 3.
note.words: Say: "What goes with 3 to make 10? Seven. So 13 and 7 make 20." On two ten frames: "One frame is full. In the other, 3 are filled. How many are empty?" Write the pair of facts: "3 + 7 = 10. 13 + 7 = 20."
note.watch: Watch who uses the partners of 10. A child who counts on by ones for every bond should go back to the bonds of 10; this page reaches into first grade and is not for everyone yet.

lessons.title: Odd or even?
lessons.objective: Children pair up the pictures in a group and say that the number is even when every one has a partner and odd when one is left over.

screen.title: Even or Odd?

note.mistake: Children circle three pictures together or leave out a picture that is far away, so they end with a leftover that should not be there, or with none when there should be one. Some think "odd" means strange.
note.words: Say: "Two by two. Does everyone have a partner?" Then name it: "No one is left over. Six is EVEN." "One is left over. Seven is ODD." Line the class up in pairs to see it.
note.watch: Check that every circle holds exactly two. This is a first look at a second-grade idea, an extra for a class that is ready: the goal is careful pairing, not knowing by heart which numbers are odd.

units.subject: math
units.title: Doubles, Three Addends, and Addition Pyramids
units.metaTitle: Grade 1 Lesson Plans: Doubles, Three Addends, and Addition Pyramids
units.metaDescription: A three-week Grade 1 math unit: 4 lessons on doubles and halves, odd and even numbers, adding three groups, and addition pyramids (number walls), with teacher notes.

lessons.title: Doubles and halves
lessons.objective: Children double a group of pictures and split an even group into two equal halves, writing the numbers.

screen.title: Doubles to 14

note.mistake: Children think doubling means adding 2, so the double of 6 becomes 8. For half, they take some away and do not check that the two parts are the same; half of 10 becomes 4 and 6.
note.words: Say: "Double means the same again. Six and six more." Use two hands: "Show me 4 on each hand." For half: "Half means two EQUAL parts. One for you, one for me, until they are gone. Are the two parts the same?"
note.watch: Watch who knows the doubles to 5 + 5 without counting and who still counts every picture; the page goes on to 7 + 7. Children who count should build each double on two hands or in two rows of a ten frame and say it: "4 and 4 is 8." On the halves page, look at the two parts a child writes: they must match.

lessons.title: Odd and even numbers
lessons.objective: Children count a group in pairs or share it between two friends, and say whether the number is odd or even.

paper.title: Odd or Even? Count the Pictures in Pairs

screen.title: Even or Odd?

exit.title: Odd or Even? Count the Pictures in Pairs

note.mistake: Children decide by how the number looks ("11 is even because it has two ones") and skip the pairing. When sharing, they forget to write the one that is left, or they give it to one of the friends.
note.words: Ask: "Can two friends share them fairly? Is one left over?" Say: "Even numbers share fairly. Odd numbers leave one over." Tie it to the doubles: "8 is 4 and 4. Every even number is a double." Have children count by twos as they circle: "2, 4, 6… and one more makes 7."
note.watch: Notice who begins to see the rule in the ones place: numbers that end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8 are even. Let children find that rule from their own pages before you say it.

lessons.title: Add three groups
lessons.objective: Children add three groups of pictures and write the total, adding an easy pair first.

screen.title: Add Three Numbers — Three-Part Number Bond

note.mistake: Children add the first two groups, write that number, and forget the third. Or they count every picture from 1 and never use a fact they know, such as a double or a pair that makes 10.
note.words: Say: "Three groups. Add two of them first, then add the third." Ask: "Which two are easy to add first? Do you see a double? Do you see a ten?" Show that you may choose the pair: "4 + 3 + 6. I add 4 and 6 first. That is 10. And 3 more is 13."
note.watch: Watch who looks for an easy pair before adding. Ask a child to tell you which two numbers were added first and why; the reason matters more than the speed.

lessons.title: Addition pyramids (number walls)
lessons.objective: Children fill a number wall in which each brick is the sum of the two bricks under it, and find a missing bottom brick.

paper.title: Number Walls: Find the Missing Brick

screen.title: Number Walls to 10

note.mistake: Children add two bricks that sit side by side and write the sum next to them, not above them. When a bottom brick is missing, they add the two numbers they can see and do not ask what is missing.
note.words: Some books call this a number pyramid. Point with two fingers under one brick: "This brick sits on these two. It is their sum." For a missing brick: "7 sits on 4 and what? Four and how many make seven?" Say "sum" for the brick on top.
note.watch: Look at the walls with a missing bottom brick. A child who writes 11 beside a 4 under a 7 has added again. Ask: "Can a brick below be bigger than the brick on top of it?"

units.subject: math
units.title: Tens and Ones
units.metaTitle: Grade 1 Math Lesson Plans: Tens and Ones
units.metaDescription: A two-week Grade 1 math unit: 4 lessons on tens and ones, number words, comparing two-digit numbers, and the number of the day, each with a teacher note.

lessons.title: Tens and ones
lessons.objective: Children read a two-digit number shown with base-ten blocks (tens rods and ones cubes), and choose the blocks that show a number.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten
Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Tens and Ones

note.mistake: Children count every rod as 1, so 3 rods and 4 cubes make 7. Or they write the digits in the order they counted them: 4 cubes and then 3 rods becomes 43.
note.words: Count the rods by tens and the cubes by ones: "10, 20, 30… 31, 32, 33, 34." Say: "3 tens and 4 ones is thirty-four." Ask: "What does the 3 in 34 mean?" (Three tens, or thirty; not three.)
note.watch: Watch the switch from counting by tens to counting by ones; that is where children slip. Have a child who slips touch the last rod, say "thirty," pause, and then touch the cubes: "thirty-one, thirty-two." Check numbers like 40: a child who writes 4 for four rods has left out the zero that holds the ones place.

lessons.title: Number words
lessons.objective: Children read numbers and match them to their words, to twenty and for the tens to one hundred.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Number Words to 20

maker.name: Number of the Day & Number Words

note.mistake: Children mix up the teen words and the tens words: thirteen and thirty, fifteen and fifty. Eleven, twelve, and eight are guessed from the first letter.
note.words: Say the endings clearly: "thir-TEEN is a ten and three. thir-TY is three tens." Ask: "Does it end in -teen or in -ty?" Have children underline the ending before they circle. Spell the hard ones together: eight, eleven, twelve, forty.
note.watch: Listen while a child reads the choices aloud. A child who reads "fifty" for fifteen is looking only at the start of the word; cover the start with a finger and read the ending first. On the tens page, check 40 and 50: "forty" and "fifty" do not look like "four" and "five."

lessons.title: Compare and order two-digit numbers
lessons.objective: Children compare two two-digit numbers with the signs for greater than and less than, and put three numbers in order.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Compare Two-Digit Numbers — Greater Than, Less Than, Equal

note.mistake: Children compare the ones digits ("29 is more than 41 because 9 is more than 1") or add the digits. The signs are mixed up too: children know which number is greater and still circle the wrong sign.
note.words: Say: "Look at the tens first. More tens means a greater number. Only if the tens are the same, look at the ones." Read the sign as words: "41 is greater than 29." The open side of the sign faces the greater number.
note.watch: Keep two questions apart: does the child know which number is greater, and does the child know the sign? Have the child say the whole sentence aloud before circling.

lessons.title: Number of the day
lessons.objective: Children show one number in many ways: as tens and ones, on ten frames, with tally marks, with its number word, and by writing 10 more and 10 less.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten
Number and Operations in Base Ten

paper.title: Number of the Day: Teen Numbers

screen.title: Tens and Ones

maker.name: Number of the Day & Number Words

note.mistake: Children fill each box as a separate task and do not notice when two boxes disagree: 15 in tens and ones, but 14 tally marks. A teen number is written as 1 and 5 with no idea that the 1 is a ten.
note.words: Ask after the page: "Do all your boxes show the same number? Prove it." Say: "Fifteen is one ten and five ones. Show me the ten in your ten frames: one full frame. Show me the ten in your tally: two bundles of five."
note.watch: Use the page as a quick look at what each child can do: which box is left empty or done last? That box tells you what to teach that child next.

units.subject: math
units.title: The Hundreds Chart and Skip Counting
units.metaTitle: Grade 1 Math Lesson Plans: The Hundreds Chart and Skip Counting
units.metaDescription: A three-week Grade 1 math unit: 4 lessons on the number line, the hundreds chart, 10 more and 10 less, and skip counting, with practice pages at three levels.

lessons.title: Find a number on the number line
lessons.objective: Children read the number an arrow points to on a number line to 20 and to 30, counting on from the nearest printed number.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

paper.title: Where on the Number Line? 0 to 30

screen.title: Whistle Valley — Number-Line Track Repair

note.mistake: Children count the tick marks beginning with 1 at zero, so every answer is one too big. When only some numbers are printed, they count from 0 for every arrow and lose count on the way.
note.words: Say: "Zero is the start, not number one. Count the JUMPS, not the marks." When few numbers are printed: "Which printed number is closest to the arrow? Start there. You can count back, too."
note.watch: Watch where a child starts for an arrow at 18. Counting back two from 20 shows a child who uses the line; counting up from 0 works but is slow. An answer that is off by exactly one means the child counted marks, not jumps: draw the jumps as hops above the line and count the hops.

lessons.title: The hundreds chart
lessons.objective: Children fill in missing numbers on a hundreds chart and use its pattern: one more to the right, ten more below.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten
Number and Operations in Base Ten

paper.title: Hundreds Chart Puzzle Pieces: Fill In the Numbers

screen.title: The Hundreds Chart

note.mistake: Children fill a gap by counting from the start of the row, or from 1. On a puzzle piece they write the next counting number in the box below (35 under 34), because they do not see that going down a row adds ten.
note.words: Run a finger down a column and read: "4, 14, 24, 34. What stays the same? What changes?" Say: "Right is one more. Down is ten more. Left is one less. Up is ten less."
note.watch: Look at the boxes below and above the printed number on a piece. A child who gets left and right and misses up and down needs the whole chart beside the page for a few more days.

lessons.title: 1 more, 1 less, 10 more, 10 less
lessons.objective: Children write the number that is 1 more and 1 less, and the number that is 10 more and 10 less, than a two-digit number.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Ten More, Ten Less — Mental Math With Two-Digit Numbers

note.mistake: For 10 more, children count on ten ones with their fingers and are often off by one. For 10 less they change the wrong digit. One more than 29 is written 210, because the child says "twenty-ten."
note.words: Ask: "Ten more than 34. Which digit changes? Which digit stays?" Say: "Ten more is one more TEN. The ones stay the same." Check on the hundreds chart only after you have written your answer.
note.watch: Watch who still counts by ones to find ten more. Check the numbers that cross a ten, such as 1 more than 39 and 1 less than 40; say those numbers aloud together before writing.

lessons.title: Count by tens, fives, and twos
lessons.objective: Children skip count by 10, by 5, and by 2, and write the missing numbers in each counting row.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Hopper's Lily Hops — Skip-Counting by 5s, 10s & 100s

note.mistake: Children say the skip-counting chant correctly and then write the next counting number in the gap (10, 20, 21). Counting by twos, they slip onto the odd numbers after one mistake and do not notice.
note.words: Count aloud as a class and stop on a number: "…30, 40. What comes next? How much more is it?" Ask about the pattern: "Counting by fives, what do the numbers end in?" (5 and 0.) "Counting by tens?" (Always 0.) "Counting by twos?" (0, 2, 4, 6, or 8: the even numbers.)
note.watch: Notice who checks a row by its pattern ("this cannot be right, it ends in 3"). Start some rows in the middle, at 40 or at 15; a child who can only begin at the start has learned a song, not a count. Three pages are a lot for one day: do tens and fives first, and twos the next day.

units.subject: math
units.title: Time, Calendar, and Coins
units.metaTitle: Grade 1 Math Lesson Plans: Time, Calendar, and Coins
units.metaDescription: A three-week Grade 1 math unit: 5 lessons on time to the hour and half hour, the calendar, ordinal numbers, and counting coins, each with a teacher note.

lessons.title: Tell time to the hour and half hour
lessons.objective: Children read a clock to the hour and to the half hour and choose the matching time.

screen.title: Sprocket's Clock — Read the Clock to the Hour

note.mistake: Children mix up the two hands and read 6:00 as 12:30. At half past, the hour hand sits between two numbers and children name the one ahead, so half past 2 is read as 3:30.
note.words: Say: "The short hand tells the hour. Read it first." At half past: "The short hand is on its way from 2 to 3. It has not reached 3, so the hour is still 2." Say it both ways: "half past two" and "two thirty."
note.watch: Ask where the hour hand points at half past and listen for "between." A child who expects it on the 3 at 2:30 should move the hands of a real clock from 2:00 to 3:00 and watch the short hand travel.

lessons.title: Draw the clock hands
lessons.objective: Children read a time to the hour or the half hour and draw the hour hand and the minute hand on a clock.

screen.title: Set the Clock — Tell Time to the Hour & Half-Hour

note.mistake: Children draw both hands the same length, so nobody can read the clock. For half past they put the hour hand exactly on the number and not halfway to the next one.
note.words: Say: "When we READ a clock, we start with the short hand. When we DRAW one, the long hand is easier to place, so draw it first: to the 12 for o'clock, to the 6 for half past. Then the hour hand: SHORT." For 4:30: "The short hand goes halfway between the 4 and the 5."
note.watch: Look at the lengths of the two hands and at where the short hand sits at half past. Drawing shows what reading hides: a child can pick 4:30 from a list and still not know where the hour hand belongs.

lessons.title: Yesterday, today, tomorrow, and the months
lessons.objective: Children write the day that was yesterday and the day that will be tomorrow, and put the twelve months in order.

paper.title: Months of the Year in Order

screen.title: Months of the Year in Order

note.mistake: Children mix up yesterday and tomorrow, and they are stuck when today is Saturday or Sunday because the week seems to end there. With the months, the order falls apart after the first few.
note.words: Say: "Yesterday is the day before today. Tomorrow is the day after." Show that the week goes around: "After Saturday comes Sunday again." Say the months in four groups of three, and ask: "Which month is your birthday in? Which month comes before it?"
note.watch: Check the items where today sits at the edge of the week: after Saturday comes Sunday, and the week starts over. For the months, notice who has to start from January each time; say the months with the calendar until the order holds from any month.

lessons.title: Ordinal numbers to tenth
lessons.objective: Children write the ordinal numbers 1st to 10th in order and match ordinal words such as third and fifth to a place in a line.

paper.title: Ordinal Words: Draw a Line to the Picture

screen.title: Write the Missing Ordinal Numbers

note.mistake: Children write 1th, 2th, 3th, or the plain number with no ending. They read "fifth" as "five" and "eighth" as "eight," and find the place by counting pictures, not by reading the word.
note.words: Teach the endings for the first ten places: "1st, 2nd, 3rd. From 4th to 10th they all end in th." Read the words aloud together: "first, second, third, fourth, fifth." Ask every time: "Where is the flag? That is where we start."
note.watch: Check the endings on 1st, 2nd, and 3rd, and whether a child starts from the flag. Reading the ordinal words is a reading task; read them with the children who cannot yet.

lessons.title: Count coins
lessons.objective: Children name a penny, a nickel, a dime, and a quarter, say what each is worth, and count the coins in a purse, starting with purses that hold one kind of coin.

screen.title: Pip's Market Stall — Counting Coins & Making Change

note.mistake: Children count the coins, not the cents: three dimes are "3." They think the nickel is worth more than the dime because it is bigger. With two kinds of coins they count everything by ones.
note.words: Hold up each coin: "A dime is small and worth 10 cents. A nickel is bigger and worth only 5." Count with the value: "10, 20, 30 cents." With two kinds: "Start with the coins that are worth the most. 10, 20… 25, 30." With a quarter: "Say 25 first, then count on: 25, 35, 45."
note.watch: Watch the switch from counting by tens to counting by fives or ones inside one purse. Children who lose the count there should stay on the first-steps page. Use real or plastic coins first; the coins on a page are hard to tell apart for children who have not handled money.

units.subject: math
units.title: Shapes, Measuring, and Graphs
units.metaTitle: Grade 1 Math Lesson Plans: Shapes, Measuring, and Graphs
units.metaDescription: A four-week Grade 1 math unit: 7 lessons on shapes, tangram puzzles, measuring length, sorting, picture graphs, bar graphs, and patterns, with teacher notes.

lessons.title: What makes a shape that shape?
lessons.objective: Children decide by its sides and corners whether a shape really is a triangle, a rectangle, or a square, and write the names of shapes.

screen.title: Defining Attributes of Shapes — Is It Still a Triangle?

note.mistake: Children accept a shape with a curved side or an open corner as a triangle because it "looks like one," and reject a real triangle that is long, thin, or turned. Color and size are taken as part of what a shape is.
note.words: Ask: "What MUST a triangle have?" (Three straight sides, three corners, and it is closed.) "Does it matter if it is big, red, or turned?" (No.) Have children give the reason: "It is not a triangle because this side is curved."
note.watch: Listen for reasons that name sides and corners. A child who says "it is too pointy" or "it is upside down" is still going by looks. A square is also a rectangle; accept that answer and say why.

lessons.title: Tangram puzzles
lessons.objective: Children build a figure with the seven tangram pieces and find the piece that is missing from a figure.

paper.title: Tangram Puzzles: Four Shadows to Build
Tangram Puzzles: Which Piece Is Missing?

screen.title: Mim's Glow Workshop — Compose Shapes from Pattern Blocks

note.mistake: Children place the big pieces last and have no room left, or they leave a piece over and call the figure finished. For the missing piece they pick one with the right shape and the wrong size.
note.words: Say: "Start with the two big triangles. Where could they go?" Ask: "Did you use all seven? Is anything sticking out?" For the missing piece: "Right shape AND right size. Turn it in your head."
note.watch: These shadow puzzles have no lines inside and are hard: let children work in pairs, and give a child who is stuck one piece placed for them, not the whole answer. Each child or pair needs a tangram set; if you have none, print and cut the page "Tangram Puzzles: Cut Out the Pieces and Build Two Figures" from the Kindergarten unit on shapes.

lessons.title: Measure length with squares
lessons.objective: Children measure the length of an object by counting the unit squares under it, and put three objects in order from shortest to longest.

screen.title: Inchie's Garden Path — Measuring by Laying Units

note.mistake: Children count every square in the row, also the ones the object does not reach, or they count the lines and not the squares. When ordering, they go by where an object ends on the page and not by how long it is.
note.words: Say: "Count only the squares under the object, from its start to its end." Say the unit every time: "The pencil is 6 squares long." Ask: "Which is longer? How many squares longer?"
note.watch: Listen for an answer with no unit ("6") and ask "six what?" Check an object that does not start at the edge of the row; that is where children count too many.

lessons.title: Sort into three groups
lessons.objective: Children decide where each picture belongs and sort a set of pictures into three groups.

screen.title: Mim's Memory Baskets — Sort Things into Groups

note.mistake: Children sort by something of their own (color, or what they like) and not by the three groups on the page. A picture that could go two ways stops them, or gets two lines.
note.words: Read the three bins first: "What goes in this one? What is the rule?" Ask for the reason with each line: "Why does the apple go there?" Afterward: "Which bin has the most? Which has the fewest?"
note.watch: Listen to the reasons more than you check the lines. A child who can say the rule for a bin is classifying; a child who matches by looks alone will be lost when the pictures change.

lessons.title: Sort, count, and read a picture graph
lessons.objective: Children count each kind in a mixed set, write the totals in a table, and read how many a picture graph shows in each row.

screen.title: Sort and Count

note.mistake: Children write a total in the wrong row of the table because they do not check the picture at the start of the row. The pages ask only for totals; when you add the question "how many more," children give the bigger number and not the difference.
note.words: Say: "Each picture in the graph stands for one thing." Ask three kinds of questions: "How many apples? Which has the most? How many MORE apples than pears?" For "how many more," line up the two rows and count the extra ones.
note.watch: Ask every child one "how many more" question; it is the hard one. See who compares two rows by matching them and who just reads off the larger number.

lessons.title: Read and make a bar graph
lessons.objective: Children read the number each bar shows and color a bar graph, one box for each one counted.

screen.title: Pip's Stacking Fence — Build & Read a Bar Graph

note.mistake: Children count the boxes in a bar and skip the bottom box, or count the line at the top as one more, so the number is off by one. They do not follow the top of the bar across to the number on the side.
note.words: Say: "Put your finger on the top of the bar. Slide it across to the numbers. What number is it on?" When coloring: "Start at the bottom. One box for each one. Stop at the number."
note.watch: See who uses the numbers on the side and who counts boxes one by one; both work, but the numbers on the side are the new idea. Check that colored bars start at the bottom and have no gaps.

lessons.title: Patterns: two are missing
lessons.objective: Children find the part that repeats in a pattern and fill in two missing pictures.

note.mistake: Children fill both empty boxes with the same picture, or look only at the picture right before each gap. A gap in the middle of the row is harder than one at the end.
note.words: Read the row aloud and clap at each empty box: "star, moon, star, (clap), star, moon." Ask: "What is the part that repeats? Say it. Now what belongs in the gap?" Check by reading the finished row aloud.
note.watch: Notice who reads the whole row again after filling the gaps. That check catches most mistakes; teach it as the last step of every pattern.

units.subject: math
units.title: Place Value to 1,000
units.metaTitle: Grade 2 Math Lesson Plans: Place Value to 1,000
units.metaDescription: A four-week Grade 2 math unit: 8 lessons that review tens and ones and skip counting, then teach hundreds, tens, and ones, comparing, and 100 more and 100 less.

lessons.title: Bundle ten ones
lessons.objective: Children circle 10 ones to make a ten and write how many tens and ones there are.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Bundle Bot — Make a Ten from Ten Ones

note.mistake: Children circle a group of about ten without counting, or they bundle a ten and then count its ones again as ones. Fourteen is written as 1 ten and 14 ones.
note.words: Say: "Ten ones make one ten. Circle exactly ten. Check." Then: "The ones inside the circle are a ten now. Count only the ones that are left outside." Ask: "Can you make another ten? How do you know?" Finish with the second-grade step: "Ten tens make one hundred."
note.watch: See who counts only the loose ones after bundling and who counts them all again. With real cubes, have children snap ten together; the page comes after the hands.

lessons.title: Count by fives and tens
lessons.objective: Children count by fives to 50 and by tens to 100, joining dots in that order to finish a picture.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Hopper's Lily Hops — Skip-Counting by 5s, 10s & 100s

note.mistake: Children know the chant from its start but cannot go on from a number in the middle. In a dot-to-dot they join the nearest dot, or read 15 and 50 as the same number.
note.words: Say: "Say the number you are on. Add five in your head. Find that number, then draw." Count by fives and by tens on a hundreds chart and ask: "What do you notice about the ones digit?" Try tens from 3: "3, 13, 23."
note.watch: Stop a child in the middle of the picture and ask what comes next. A child who starts the chant over from 5 knows a song; counting on from 35 is the skill. The pages stop at 50 and at 100, and second graders skip count to 1,000, so end with a spoken round that starts past 100: "285, 290, 295…", "340, 350, 360…", "200, 300, 400…".

lessons.title: A number line that does not start at zero
lessons.objective: Children read the number an arrow points to on a number line that starts at 40 or at 60 and has only some of its numbers printed.

paper.title: Where on the Number Line? 40 to 60
Where on the Number Line? 60 to 100

screen.title: Whistle Valley — Number-Line Track Repair

exit.title: Where on the Number Line? 40 to 60

note.mistake: Children count the marks from the left end as 1, 2, 3, as if the line began at zero. Or they start at a printed number and count that mark as the first jump, landing one off.
note.words: Ask before anything else: "Where does this line start? What is each jump worth?" Say: "Find the nearest printed number. Count on from it, or count back." Check: "Is your number between the two printed numbers around it?"
note.watch: Look for answers such as 3 or 7 on a line from 40 to 60; that child ignored the printed numbers. Have each child tell you the start number and the size of one jump before writing.

lessons.title: Jumps on the hundreds chart
lessons.objective: Children follow arrows on a hundreds chart, adding or taking away tens and ones, and write the number where they land.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten
Number and Operations in Base Ten
Number and Operations in Base Ten

paper.title: Mystery Number: Two Arrows, One Square

screen.title: Ten More, Ten Less — Mental Math With Two-Digit Numbers

note.mistake: Children mix up the directions: up feels like more, so they add ten for an up arrow. With several arrows they make one jump, forget the number they reached, and start again from the first number.
note.words: Have children say each jump: "Down is ten more: 34, 44. Right is one more: 45." Ask: "Up one row. Is the number bigger or smaller? Check on the chart." Let them write the number after every arrow.
note.watch: Notice who has to look at the chart and who can make the jump mentally. Check the up arrows first; a child who adds on an up arrow is thinking "higher is more," as on a thermometer.

lessons.title: Hundreds, tens, and ones
lessons.objective: Children read a three-digit number shown with hundreds, tens, and ones blocks and fill in a place-value chart.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Hundreds, Tens, and Ones

note.mistake: Children write the counts they see and skip an empty place: two flats and six cubes become 26. When a number is read aloud, the same children write what they hear, and two hundred six becomes 2006.
note.words: Count by place: "100, 200… 210, 220… 221, 222." Say: "Every place needs a digit. No tens? Write a zero to hold the place." Ask: "What is the 2 worth in 206? And the 0? And the 6?"
note.watch: Check every number with a zero in the tens or the ones place first. A child who writes 26 for two flats and six cubes should keep the place-value chart beside every number for now.

lessons.title: Expanded form and the value of a digit
lessons.objective: Children match a set of hundreds, tens, and ones blocks to its expanded form and tell what an underlined digit is worth.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten
Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Expanded Form

note.mistake: Children say an underlined 4 is worth "4" wherever it is. For 345 they pick 300 + 4 + 5, treating the tens digit as ones.
note.words: Ask: "What place is the digit in? The tens place, so it is 4 tens. What are 4 tens worth?" (40.) Say a number in parts: "345 is 300 and 40 and 5." Write it both ways and read it both ways.
note.watch: Ask for the value of the same digit in two places, as in 44 or 404. A child who answers "four" both times is naming the digit, not its value.

lessons.title: Compare and order three-digit numbers
lessons.objective: Children compare two three-digit numbers with the signs for greater than, less than, and equal, and put four numbers in order.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Compare Three-Digit Numbers

note.mistake: Children decide by the biggest digit anywhere in the number ("199 is greater than 201 because of the nines"). When the hundreds are the same, they jump to the ones and skip the tens.
note.words: Say: "Start on the left. Compare the hundreds. Same? Then the tens. Same? Then the ones." Read the finished line aloud: "402 is greater than 398." For ordering: "Find the least number and write 1 by it. Then find the least of the ones that are left."
note.watch: Use pairs like 398 and 402 to see who compares place by place from the left. In ordering four numbers, look for a child who compares only neighbors and never checks the whole row.

lessons.title: 100 more, 100 less
lessons.objective: Children write the number that is 100 less and the number that is 100 more than a three-digit number.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Comet's Big Leaps — 10 & 100 More or Less

note.mistake: Children change the tens or the ones digit, or count up by ones and give up. A hundred less than a number just over 100, such as 105, leaves them without a hundreds digit and unsure what to write.
note.words: Ask: "A hundred more. Which digit changes? Which two stay the same?" Say: "Only the hundreds digit changes. 347, 447." Count by hundreds from any number: "26, 126, 226, 326." Then try ten: "347, 357. Which digit changed this time?"
note.watch: See who answers at once by changing one digit and who still counts. Give one number above 900 and talk about what comes after 9 hundreds.

units.subject: math
units.title: Adding and Subtracting Within 100 and 1,000
units.metaTitle: Grade 2 Math Lesson Plans: Adding and Subtracting Within 100 and 1,000
units.metaDescription: A two-week Grade 2 math unit: 4 lessons on adding and subtracting with blocks, vertically, and in addition pyramids and a maze, each with a teacher note.

lessons.title: Add with blocks
lessons.objective: Children add two groups of hundreds, tens, and ones blocks and write the total.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Tuck Makes a Hundred — Add with Regrouping

note.mistake: Children count each kind of block and write the three counts side by side, even when there are 12 ones or 11 tens: 2 hundreds, 4 tens, and 12 ones become 2412.
note.words: Say: "Put the ones together first. Are there ten or more? Trade ten ones for one ten." Then the tens: "Ten tens? Trade them for a hundred." Ask: "How many ones are left after the trade?"
note.watch: Look for answers with four digits where three are expected; they show a missed trade. Use real blocks and make the trade with the hands before anything is written.

lessons.title: Subtract with blocks
lessons.objective: Children take one group of blocks away from another and write how many are left.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Tuck Breaks a Ten — Subtract with Regrouping

note.mistake: When there are not enough ones to take away, children take the smaller digit from the bigger one in each place (52 − 17 becomes 45), or they say it cannot be done.
note.words: Say: "I need to take 7 ones and I have only 2. Trade one ten for ten ones. Now I have 12 ones." Ask: "How many tens are left after the trade?" Cross out blocks on the page as they are taken away.
note.watch: Check the problems where the second number has more ones than the first. A child who writes the difference of the digits should break a real ten-rod into ones a few times.

lessons.title: Add and subtract vertically
lessons.objective: Children add and subtract two-digit numbers written in columns, starting with the ones and writing the traded ten.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

screen.title: Tuck's Ten Bundles — Add with Regrouping

note.mistake: Children write a two-digit sum under the ones column (27 + 15 becomes 312), or they write the new ten and forget to add it. Children who add the tens first have nowhere to put the new ten and leave the tens digit as it was. In subtraction they still take the smaller digit from the bigger one, as with the blocks.
note.words: Say: "Ones first. 7 and 5 is 12 ones: 1 ten and 2 ones. Write the 2, and write the new ten above the tens." In subtraction: "2 ones take away 7? Not enough ones. Trade one ten for ten ones: now there are 12 ones." Have children say what the small 1 means: "one ten," not "one."
note.watch: Ask a child to explain the small carried digit. If it is "just a one," go back to blocks and make the trade. Compare the answer with an estimate: "About how much should it be?"

lessons.title: Add and subtract within 100
lessons.objective: Children add and subtract two-digit numbers to fill number walls and to follow a road through a math maze.

standards.title: Number and Operations in Base Ten

paper.title: Math Maze for 2nd Grade: Add and Subtract Within 100

screen.title: Gus's Snack Cart — Add & Subtract Within 100

note.mistake: Children add the tens and the ones and forget to trade when the ones make more than 9: 28 + 15 becomes 313 or 33. In the maze one wrong step carries along the whole road, and they do not go back to find it.
note.words: Say: "Add the tens, add the ones, then put them together. 28 + 15: 30, and 13 more, 43." Ask: "Do the ones make a new ten?" In the maze: "Write the number after every sign. If the end is wrong, check each step."
note.watch: Let children show their steps beside the wall. A child with the lower bricks right and one brick near the top wrong made a single adding mistake that carried upward; a child with nothing right may not see which two bricks to add.

units.subject: math
units.title: Measurement, Time, and Money
units.metaTitle: Grade 2 Math Lesson Plans: Measurement, Time, and Money
units.metaDescription: A four-week Grade 2 math unit: 5 lessons on measuring with a ruler, time to the nearest five minutes, the calendar, and money, each with a teacher note.

lessons.title: Measure with a ruler
lessons.objective: Children read the length of an object on a ruler when the object starts at 0, and write the number of units.

screen.title: Tildy's Tailor Shop — Measure with a Ruler

note.mistake: Children count the number marks and not the spaces, so they say "one" at the zero mark and read one too many. With a real ruler they line the object up with the edge of the ruler or with the 1, not with the 0.
note.words: Say: "Start at zero. Zero means no length yet. Count the spaces: one, two, three." Then: "The end of the pencil is at the 6, so it is 6 units long." With a real ruler: "Find the 0 mark. It is not always at the edge. Are we using the inch side or the centimeter side? Say the unit: 6 inches."
note.watch: Hand out real rulers and look at where children put the start of the object. The page starts everything at 0; a classroom ruler does not do that for them.

lessons.title: How much longer?
lessons.objective: Children measure two objects and find how many units longer one is than the other.

screen.title: Span's Length Gap — How Much Longer?

note.mistake: Children write the length of the longer object as the answer to "how much longer." Or they add the two lengths, because two numbers in a problem have always meant adding.
note.words: Say: "The ribbon is 9 units long. The string is 6 units long. Line them up. Where does the string stop? The extra part is how much LONGER." Write it: "9 − 6 = 3. The ribbon is 3 units longer."
note.watch: Ask the child to show the extra part with two fingers on the page. A child who can show it and cannot write the subtraction needs the words "how many more to get from 6 to 9."

lessons.title: Tell time to the nearest five minutes
lessons.objective: Children read a clock to the nearest five minutes and to the quarter hour and choose the matching time.

screen.title: Sprocket's Clock — Read the Clock to Five Minutes

note.mistake: Children read the number the minute hand points to as the minutes: a hand on the 4 is "4 minutes," and 2:20 becomes 2:04. Near the end of an hour they name the next hour: 2:50 is read as 3:50.
note.words: Count by fives around the clock, touching each number: "5, 10, 15, 20." Say: "The 4 means 20 minutes." For the hour: "Has the short hand passed the 3 yet? No, so it is still 2." Use both names: "2:15" and "quarter past two." Add the half of the day: "School ends at 2:15. Is that a.m. or p.m.?"
note.watch: Check times after the half hour, such as 2:50, where the hour hand is almost on the next number. Have the child count by fives aloud once; you will hear where it goes wrong.

lessons.title: Read a calendar
lessons.objective: Children read a month calendar to find the weekday of a date, the date one week later, and the number of days between two dates.

paper.title: Read the Calendar: A First Look
Read the Calendar: A Busy Month

screen.title: Read the Calendar: A First Look

exit.title: Read the Calendar: A First Look

note.mistake: Children read along a row to find a weekday and do not look up to the top of the column. For "one week later" they count seven boxes one by one and often count the starting day as day one.
note.words: Say: "Find the date. Go straight up the column. What day is at the top?" For a week later: "One week later is the box right below. Same weekday, 7 more." Counting days: "Do not count the day you start on. Count the jumps."
note.watch: Ask "What day of the week is the 17th?" and follow the child's finger: it should travel up the column. Check "how many days from… to…" answers that are one too many.

lessons.title: Shopping with money
lessons.objective: Children read prices from a shelf, add the prices of the things in a basket, and solve two story problems with those prices.

paper.title: Shopping Math: Add Up the Basket

screen.title: Make Change with Coins — Money Word Problems

exit.title: Shopping Math: Add Up the Basket

note.mistake: Children add numbers without checking which thing the story names, or take the price of the wrong thing from the shelf. With three things in a basket they add two prices and forget the third.
note.words: Say: "First find each thing on the shelf and say its price. Write the prices down. Then add." Ask: "How much does it cost altogether?" Say amounts with the unit: "45 cents."
note.watch: Have children underline what is being bought before they look at the shelf. Check that totals carry a cent sign or a dollar sign; a bare number is half an answer. Have one child in each group lay out a total with coins on the Money Mat, because the pages never show a coin.

units.subject: math
units.title: Graphs and Grids
units.metaTitle: Grade 2 Math Lesson Plans: Graphs and Grids
units.metaDescription: A two-week Grade 2 math unit: 4 lessons on bar graphs and line plots, plus a first look at picture graphs with a key and at squares on a grid, each with a teacher note.

lessons.title: From tally marks to a bar graph
lessons.objective: Children read a tally chart, color a bar for each count, and use a bar graph to answer questions that put together or compare.
