paper.title: ABC Order: When Words Start the Same

screen.title: ABC Order: Number the Words

note.mistake: Children order the words by where they think the letter comes in the song and lose track in the middle of the alphabet. When two words start with the same letter, they stop or order them by length.
note.words: Say: "Look only at the first letter. Find each one on the alphabet strip. Which comes first on the strip?" For a tie: "Both start with b. Cover the b. Now look at the next letter."
note.watch: Keep the alphabet strip in sight; the goal is using the order, not reciting it. Check the pairs that start alike: a child who numbers "bed" before "bat" has not moved on to the second letter; cover the first letters and ask again.

lessons.title: Nouns, verbs, and adjectives
lessons.objective: Children sort words into nouns and verbs, and into nouns and adjectives.

screen.title: Nouns and Verbs: Two Bins

note.mistake: Children sort by what a word makes them think of: "party" and "game" go with the verbs because you do something there, and "fast" or "hungry" goes with the verbs because it happens to you. Words that can be both (a walk, to walk) confuse them, and rightly so.
note.words: Give each kind a test sentence: "A noun is a person, place, animal, or thing. Try it here: 'I see the ___.' I see the dog. A verb is something you can do. Try it here: 'I can ___.' I can jump. An adjective tells what something is like. Try it here: 'The dog is very ___.' The dog is very big."
note.watch: Have children use the test aloud for the hard words. If a child argues that "paint" can be both, the child is right; say so and ask for a sentence each way.

lessons.title: He, she, it, they
lessons.objective: Children choose the pronoun that takes the place of a name and write it in a sentence.

paper.title: Replace the Name with a Pronoun

screen.title: The Borrowed Hat — Personal Pronouns

note.mistake: Children write the name again in the second sentence, or use "they" only for a crowd and not for two people. They are unsure about "it" for an animal or a thing. Children who are learning English may use "he" for everyone or mix up "he" and "she."
note.words: Say: "We do not say the name over and over. 'Ben has a kite. Ben flies the kite' becomes 'Ben has a kite. HE flies it.'" Ask: "Who is 'he' in this sentence? Point to the name." For two people: "Ben and Mia: they." For a thing: "The kite: it."
note.watch: Have the child read both sentences aloud and tell you who the pronoun means. Children learning English may not have he and she in their home language; give them more spoken practice.

lessons.title: A or an: sort the words
lessons.objective: Children read a word, decide whether a or an belongs in front of it, and write it in the right group.

screen.title: Sort the Words

note.mistake: Children put every word under "a," because "a" is the word they use most, or they stop reading and fill the two groups evenly. A child who sorts correctly by the first letter has the right answers here and will go wrong later on words such as "hour" and "unicorn," where the letter and the sound do not agree.
note.words: Say: "Read the word. Say its first sound. Is it a vowel sound? Then it goes under an." Check by ear: "A egg… an egg. Which one do we say?" Have children read each finished group aloud: "an apple, an egg, an owl."
note.watch: Listen to the child read the finished lists with the article in front. A wrong word stands out at once when it is said aloud; have the child find it by ear, not by rule.

lessons.title: Write the opposite
lessons.objective: Children find the opposite of a word in a word bank and tell an opposite from a word that means the same.

paper.title: Opposite or the Same? Circle the Opposite

screen.title: Quill's Mirror Market — Find the Opposite

note.mistake: Children circle the word that means the same, because it is the word that "goes with" the first one. On the word bank page they take a word that is about the same thing and is not the opposite, such as "warm" for "hot."
note.words: Say: "Opposite means as different as can be: hot, cold. Same means nearly alike: big, large." Test a word with "not": "If the door is not open, it is… shut. So open and shut are opposites." Ask: "Is that word the opposite, or does it mean the same?"
note.watch: On the three-word page, a child who circles the same-meaning word knows the words are related and has not sorted out how. Ask for both: "Which one means the same? Which one is the opposite?"

lessons.title: Two words that mean the same thing
lessons.objective: Children look at a picture and circle the two words under it that mean the same and tell about the picture.

paper.title: Synonyms with Pictures: Two Words, One Picture

screen.title: Synonyms with Pictures: Two Words, One Picture

exit.title: Synonyms with Pictures: Two Words, One Picture

note.mistake: Children circle two words that both fit the picture and do not mean the same (big and gray for an elephant), or they circle a word and its opposite, because opposites also belong together.
note.words: Say: "Words that mean the same can trade places. The big dog, the large dog: same picture in your head." Test a pair in one sentence: "The elephant is big. The elephant is large. Same? The elephant is gray. Same?" Call them "words that mean the same," and give the word "synonyms" once.
note.watch: Have the child say both circled words in one sentence about the picture. If the meaning changes from one sentence to the other, the words are not synonyms; have the child keep one word and test it against each of the others.

lessons.title: From a little to a lot
lessons.objective: Children put three words with nearly the same meaning in order from the weakest to the strongest.

paper.title: Shades of Meaning: From a Little to a Lot

screen.title: Pesto's Soup Stall — Shades of Meaning

exit.title: Shades of Meaning: From a Little to a Lot

note.mistake: Children treat the three words as meaning exactly the same and number them in the order printed. They know the plain word (big) and are unsure of the strong one (enormous).
note.words: Act the words out or show them with your hands: "Show me cool. Show me cold. Show me freezing." Ask: "Which one is the most? Which is only a little?" Use them in one sentence: "The water is cool… cold… freezing!"
note.watch: Ask which word of a row the child did not know. Ordering three words is easy once the words are known; the lesson is really about learning the strong word.

lessons.title: Find the root word
lessons.objective: Children name a picture and find the longer word that is built from that word, such as rain in rainy.

paper.title: Root Words with Pictures: Circle the Word

screen.title: Sage's Root Garden — Find the Root Word Family

exit.title: Root Words with Pictures: Circle the Word

note.mistake: Children circle a word that only starts with the same letters as the picture word and has nothing to do with it: "carrot" for the picture of a car, "panda" for the picture of a pan.
note.words: Say: "A root word is the word a longer word is built from, and the meaning stays. Rain, rainy, raining: all about rain." Test it: "Does a carrot have anything to do with a car? No. So 'carrot' is not built from 'car.'"
note.watch: Ask the child what the long word means. If the meaning has the picture word in it (a teacher teaches), the root is right; if not, the letters match by accident.

units.subject: literacy
units.title: Sentences and Grammar
units.metaTitle: Grade 2 Reading and Writing Lesson Plans: Sentences and Grammar
units.metaDescription: A three-week Grade 2 unit: 6 lessons on capital letters and end marks, parts of speech (nouns, verbs, adjectives), plurals, verb forms, pronouns, and writing questions.

lessons.title: Capital letters and end marks
lessons.objective: Children rewrite a sentence with its capital letter and its end mark, and split two sentences that ran together.

paper.title: Fix the Sentence: Where Does It End?

screen.title: Dr. Plume's Sentence Clinic — Fix-the-Sentence Grammar

note.mistake: Children add the period and forget the capital, or the other way around. With two sentences run together, they put the period where they would take a breath, and one of the two "sentences" has no verb.
note.words: Say: "A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a mark. Both, every time." For run-on sentences: "Read it aloud. Where does the first idea stop? Who is the second sentence about?" Test each part: "Does it tell who or what, and what happens?"
note.watch: Have the child read each of the two new sentences alone. If one of them does not make sense by itself, the break is in the wrong place. Check that the second sentence got its own capital letter.

lessons.title: Nouns, verbs, and adjectives: three bins
lessons.objective: Children sort words into nouns, verbs, and adjectives and write each word in its bin.

screen.title: Nouns, Verbs, and Adjectives

note.mistake: Children put a word in a bin by a feeling ("happy" is a verb because you can "be happy"). Words that can be two things (a drink, to drink; a play, to play) are sorted one way with no second thought.
note.words: Give three test sentences: "Noun: can you say 'I see the ___' or 'I have some ___'? Verb: can you say 'I can ___' or 'She ___s every day'? Adjective: can you say 'The thing is very ___'?" For a word that fits two bins: "Use it in a sentence. Now which is it?"
note.watch: Ask for a sentence with any word a child placed in a surprising bin; a good sentence can make the child right. Adjectives are the weakest bin for most children, so check that bin first.

lessons.title: More than one: plural nouns
lessons.objective: Children write the plural of a noun, with -s, with -es, and for nouns that change, such as mouse and mice.

paper.title: Fill in the Blank: Plural Nouns

screen.title: The Doubling Pond — Irregular Plural Nouns

exit.title: Fill in the Blank: Plural Nouns

note.mistake: Children add -s to everything: "foxs," "mouses," "childs." The opposite also happens: after learning the new word, a child marks the plural twice and writes "mices," "feets," or "childrens."
note.words: Say the plural aloud first: "One fox, two foxes. Do you hear the extra beat? Then it needs -es. If the word already ends in e, as in horse, just add s." For the ones that change: "These you have to know: one mouse, two mice; one child, two children; one foot, two feet." Keep a class list of them.
note.watch: Sort a child's errors: -s where -es belongs is a spelling rule to teach; "mouses" is a word to learn by heart. The two need different help.

lessons.title: Today and yesterday: verb forms
lessons.objective: Children write the present and the past form of a verb, including be, have, do, and go, and use the right form in a sentence.

paper.title: The Irregular Verbs: be, have, do, go

screen.title: Rusty's Yesterday Machine — Irregular Past-Tense Verbs

note.mistake: Children add -ed to every verb: "goed," "runned," "haved." With "be" they do not see that am, is, are, was, and were are all one verb.
note.words: Use two sentence frames all through: "Today I ___. Yesterday I ___." Say them aloud: "Today I go. Yesterday I went." For be: "Today I am, you are, she is. Yesterday I was, you were, she was." Ask: "Does it sound right?"
note.watch: Listen for the forms children use when they talk; many say "went" and still write "goed" when a page asks for an ending. Have them read their sentence aloud and listen. The ear helps only children who hear these forms every day; for children learning English, or whose home speech uses other forms ("he do," "we was"), teach the forms from a class chart without calling the home form wrong. In the sentences, check has, does, and goes after he, she, or it.

lessons.title: Who does the pronoun stand for?
lessons.objective: Children find the name a pronoun stands for and rewrite a sentence with a pronoun in place of the name.

paper.title: Who Is He? Pronouns in Sentences
Rewrite the Sentence with a Pronoun

screen.title: Who Is He? Pronouns in Sentences

exit.title: Who Is He? Pronouns in Sentences

note.mistake: Children link a pronoun to the nearest name, not to the one it means: in "Sam gave Lily his book," "his" is tied to Lily. When rewriting, they pick the wrong form ("Him went home").
note.words: Ask: "Who is 'she' here? Put the name back in. Does the sentence still say the same thing?" For rewriting: "Is the person doing the action? Then he, she, or they. Is something done to the person? Then him, her, or them. Does something belong to the person? Then his, her, or their."
note.watch: Use the put-the-name-back test on each line a child drew. Read rewritten sentences aloud together; "Him went home" sounds wrong to most children once they hear it.

lessons.title: Write the question
lessons.objective: Children write a question that asks for a given answer, choosing among who, what, where, when, why, and how.

paper.title: Ask About the Picture: Why and How

screen.title: Write the Question

note.mistake: Children write a statement with a question mark at the end ("The dog is in the yard?"), or they start with the right question word and keep the word order of a statement ("Where the dog is?"). When the sentence has an action verb, they leave out "does" or "did" ("What Maya eats?").
note.words: Say: "The highlighted words are the ANSWER. Which question word asks for a place? A reason? A way of doing it?" Build it aloud: "The dog is in the yard. Where… is the dog?" Point out the switch: "is the dog," not "the dog is." With an action verb: "Maya eats an apple. What DOES Maya eat?"
note.watch: Read a child's question and answer it yourself with the highlighted words. If your answer does not fit the question, the question word is wrong. Check for the question mark last.

units.subject: literacy
units.title: Spelling, Word Building, and Word Choice
units.metaTitle: Grade 2 Lesson Plans: Spelling, Word Building, and Word Choice
units.metaDescription: A three-week Grade 2 unit: 6 lessons that review the digraph sh, then teach spelling rules, compound words, root words, synonyms, and more exact words for "said."

lessons.title: Review: find sh in sentences
lessons.objective: Children read sentences, circle every sh, including the ones in the middle and at the end of a word, and count them.

paper.title: Digraphs in Sentences: Circle and Count sh

screen.title: Build Blend and Digraph Words

exit.title: Digraphs in Sentences: Circle and Count sh

note.mistake: Children find sh at the start of words and miss it in the middle and at the end (fishing, brush). Some circle every s and every h they see, even when the two letters are not side by side.
note.words: Say: "sh is a team: the two letters are side by side and make one sound." Read each sentence aloud slowly and have children raise a hand when they HEAR /sh/. Then: "Now find it with your eyes. Beginning, middle, or end?" Add: "If you hear /sh/ and cannot find sh, as in 'sure,' tell me: that word spells the sound another way."
note.watch: Compare the number in the box with the number of circles. A child who reads silently misses more; have that child whisper the sentence. Check words like "fish" and "washing," where the team is not at the start.

lessons.title: Spelling rules: which letters go here?
lessons.objective: Children read a spelling rule and choose the right letters for a sound by where it is in the word, for example ck after a short vowel.

screen.title: Word Doctor's Clinic — Heal the Sick Sound

note.mistake: Children spell a sound the same way everywhere: "duk" and "bike" both get a plain k. They can say the rule as a sentence and do not check the sound that comes before.
note.words: Read the rule on the page together and turn it into a question to ask each time. For ck and k, for example: "What comes right before the /k/ sound? One short vowel?" Say: "Right after one short vowel, ck: duck, sock. After anything else, just k: milk, book, bike." Have children say the word, then the sound just before /k/, then the spelling.
note.watch: Ask the child why a word got its letters. "Because of the rule" is not enough; the child should name the sound that comes before. Each page practices one rule; mix the rules only after each has been practiced alone.

lessons.title: Compound words
lessons.objective: Children join two words to make a compound word and find where a compound word splits into its two words.

paper.title: Match the Halves: Two Pictures, One Word
Split the Compound: Find the Two Words

screen.title: Skip's Word-Welding Yard — Build & Mean Compound Words

exit.title: Match the Halves: Two Pictures, One Word

note.mistake: Children split a word wherever they see a small word inside it: "car-pet," "but-ton." In a real compound they cut after the first few letters and not where the second word begins. On the matching page they join two pictures that go together in life (sun and moon) and not two that make a word (sun and flower).
note.words: Say: "A compound word is two whole words stuck together, and both still mean something: rain + coat, a coat for the rain." Test a split: "Is 'car' a word? Is 'pet' a word? Is a carpet a pet in a car? Then it is not a compound."
note.watch: Have the child say both halves and tell what the whole word means with both halves in it ("a brush for teeth"). A split that leaves a half that is not a word shows at once.

lessons.title: Root words and word families
lessons.objective: Children find the root that three words share and sort words by their root.

paper.title: Root Words: Sort by the Root

screen.title: Sage's Root Garden — Find the Root Word Family

note.mistake: Children circle only the letters that are printed the same in all three words, so the root of "baker, baking, baked" becomes "bak." Or they keep a letter that was only added for spelling: the root of "running" becomes "runn."
note.words: Say: "The root is the part that means the same in all three: play, player, playing. What do they all have to do with?" Cover the endings with a finger. For a changed spelling: "Running comes from run; the extra n is there for the spelling. Baking comes from bake; the e was dropped. Write the root the way it is spelled when it stands alone."
note.watch: Ask what the three words have in common in MEANING before the child circles. Then have the child read the root written in the stone: is it a real word by itself? "Bak" and "runn" are not, so the child goes back and repairs the spelling.

lessons.title: Synonyms
lessons.objective: Children choose and match words that mean the same, such as glad and happy.

paper.title: Synonyms: Circle the Word That Means the Same
Synonym Pairs: Match the Words That Mean the Same

screen.title: Synonyms: Circle the Word That Means the Same

exit.title: Synonyms: Circle the Word That Means the Same

note.mistake: Children pick a word that often goes with the first word (cold and ice, big and house) and not one that could take its place. On the matching page they join the easy pairs and then link the leftover words without reading them.
note.words: Give the swap test: "Put the new word in the sentence where the old one was. Does the sentence still mean the same?" Try it: "I am glad. I am happy. Same. I am glad. I am sad. Not the same." Use the word "synonym."
note.watch: Note the words nobody knew; those are vocabulary to teach first, because no test finds a synonym for a word a child has never met. Ask a child to use both words of one pair in the same sentence.

lessons.title: More exact words for "said"
lessons.objective: Children read a sentence and choose a more exact word than said, such as whispered, shouted, or asked.

paper.title: Synonyms for Said: Pick the Word That Fits

screen.title: Synonyms for Said: Pick the Word That Fits

exit.title: Synonyms for Said: Pick the Word That Fits

note.mistake: Children take the words in the order they are printed in the bubble, or use one favorite ("shouted") everywhere. They do not look for the clue in the sentence that tells how something was said.
note.words: Ask: "HOW did the person say it? Look for a clue: a question mark, an exclamation point, a word like 'quietly.'" Act it out: "Say it in a whisper. Now shout it. Which word fits what happened?"
note.watch: Have the child read the finished sentence in the voice the new word calls for. If "whispered" comes before a sentence with an exclamation point, the child will hear the clash.

units.subject: literacy
units.title: Reading Stories and Writing
units.metaTitle: Grade 2 Lesson Plans: Reading Stories and Writing
units.metaDescription: A three-week Grade 2 unit: 6 lessons on answering story questions, missing words, writing about a picture, retelling, an animal fact sheet, and a first look at cursive.

lessons.title: Read a story and answer questions
lessons.objective: Children read a short story and answer who, what, where, when, and why questions with details from the text.

screen.title: Read and Answer

note.mistake: Children answer from what they know about the world or from the first sentence they remember, without going back to the story. A wrong answer that uses a word from the story is picked because the word looks familiar.
note.words: Say: "The answer is in the story. Go back and find the sentence that tells you. Put your finger on it." Ask after each answer: "Where does it say that?" For a why question: "Look for 'because,' or for what happened just before."
note.watch: Ask a child to show the sentence that proves one answer. A child who can point to it is reading closely; one who says "I just know" is guessing, even when the answer is right.

lessons.title: Fill in the story's missing words
lessons.objective: Children read a whole short story and use what happens in it to choose the word that belongs in each blank.

screen.title: Fern's Clue Garden — Find a Word's Meaning from the Sentence

note.mistake: Children fill the first blank after reading only up to it, and choose a word that fits that one sentence and not the story. A word used wrongly early leaves the wrong word for the last blank.
note.words: Say: "Read the WHOLE story first and say 'blank' at each empty box. What is the story about?" Then: "Try a word. Read on to the next sentence. Does it still make sense?" Add: "Sometimes the clue comes after the blank, so read ahead as well as back."
note.watch: See whether a child reads to the end before writing. Have the finished story read aloud; a word in the wrong blank makes a sentence that sounds odd, and most children catch it by ear.

lessons.title: Write about a picture
lessons.objective: Children write sentences about a picture with sentence starters and a word bank, and then write their own short story about a picture with the word bank only.

paper.title: Write About the Picture: What You See
Write About the Picture: Your Own Words

exit.title: Write About the Picture: What You See

note.mistake: Children write a list ("a dog, a ball, a tree") and not sentences, or every sentence begins "I see." Words are copied from the word bank with no capital at the start of the sentence and no period.
note.words: Ask for a whole thought: "Who or what is in the picture? What is it doing? Where?" Say a sentence together before writing it: "The dog runs after the ball." Offer new beginnings: "Next to the tree…", "A girl…", "In the sky…"
note.watch: Count the different sentence beginnings on a child's page. Have the child read the writing aloud and point to each period; a missing verb shows when the sentence is read.

lessons.title: Retell a story: first, next, then, at the end
lessons.objective: Children write what happens in each picture of a story in order, beginning with the time-order word that is given.

note.mistake: Children describe each picture by itself ("There is a cat") and do not tell what HAPPENS or how one picture leads to the next. Some copy the starter word and then begin a new sentence, so the starter is left alone.
note.words: Tell the story aloud before anyone writes: "First… Next… Then… At the end…" Ask at each picture: "What happened here? Why? What changed since the last picture?" Show how the starter joins the sentence: "First, the cat climbs the tree."
note.watch: Have the child read the four parts as one story. It should make sense to someone who cannot see the pictures; if it does not, ask what the listener would need to know.

lessons.title: An animal fact sheet
lessons.objective: Children choose true facts about an animal, such as what it eats, where it lives, and how it moves, and write them on a fact sheet.

paper.title: Animal Fact File: Circle the True Facts
Animal Fact File with a Word Bank

note.mistake: Children circle what they know from stories and cartoons and not what is true: honey for the bear, cheese for the mouse. When copying from the word bank, a fact lands in the wrong row: what the animal eats is written under where it lives.
note.words: Say: "A fact is true, and we can check it in a book or by looking." Read the row names first: "What does this row ask for? Food, home, or how it moves?" Ask: "How do you know that? Where could we check?"
note.watch: Ask a child to read one row name and then the fact beside it; a fact in the wrong row sounds wrong at once. Keep a few animal books on hand and let children check one fact each.

lessons.title: Cursive letters and connections
lessons.objective: Children trace and write rows of connected cursive letters (i, t, u, and w) and connect two letters without lifting the pencil (for schools that teach cursive in Grade 2).

paper.title: Cursive Letters: i, t, u and w
Cursive Connecting Letters: Joining Two Letters

exit.title: Cursive Letters: i, t, u and w

note.mistake: Children lift the pencil after every letter and add the connecting stroke afterward, so the row is print letters with tails. Some stop in the middle of a word to dot the i or cross the t, which breaks the flow.
note.words: Say: "Keep the pencil down until the whole word is written. Then go back: dot the i, cross the t." Name the strokes: "up, down, and out to the next letter." For w: "W ends high, at the middle line, so the next letter starts from up there, not from the bottom line." Write it big in the air first, then on the page.
note.watch: Watch the pencil, not the page: is it lifted inside a word? Check that each connection starts where the letter before it ended and that the letters sit on the line. Right-handed children tilt the paper with its top to the left; left-handed children tilt it with its top to the right, so that the hand stays below the writing.

units.subject: literacy
units.title: Words and Their Meanings
units.metaTitle: Grade 3 Reading and Writing Lesson Plans: Words and Their Meanings
units.metaDescription: A two-week Grade 3 unit: 4 lessons on prefixes, more exact words for "go" and "look," words that name a person, such as "baker," and choosing the right form of a word.

lessons.title: Prefixes change the meaning
lessons.objective: Children add a prefix such as un-, dis-, re-, or mis- to a word and tell what the new word means.

paper.title: Prefixes re-, pre- and mis-: Pick by Meaning

screen.title: Marigold's Knowing Machine — Prefixes & Suffixes Word Meaning

note.mistake: Children put any prefix on any word ("unhonest," "dishappy"), or they see a prefix in a word that has none: "uncle" and "under" are taken apart. They can build the word and cannot say what it means.
note.words: Give each prefix a meaning to say: "un-, dis-, and in- mean not or the opposite of. re- means again. pre- means before. mis- means wrong or badly." Use it: "Unhappy: not happy. Dishonest: not honest. Incorrect: not correct. Reread: read again. Preheat: heat before. Misspell: spell wrong." Test a doubtful word: "Take off un-. Is 'cle' a word? Then 'uncle' has no prefix."
note.watch: Have the child explain each new word with the prefix's meaning in it. For un-, dis-, and in-, only some pairs exist; children learn those by hearing them, so say the right word back ("dishonest") and give no rule. Watch for words where in- means "in" and not "not" (inside, indoors); tell the child that this in- is a different one.

lessons.title: Words for go and words for look
lessons.objective: Children sort verbs such as stroll, dash, glance, and stare into groups by meaning and tell the close words apart.

paper.title: Word Fields: Words for Go and Look

screen.title: Roary's Roar Meter — Strongest & Weakest Words

exit.title: Word Fields: Words for Go and Look

note.mistake: Children know "go" and "look" and take the other words for the same thing said in a fancier way. A word they do not know is placed by guess or left out.
note.words: Act each word out: "Show me stroll. Show me dash. Are they both ways to go? What is different?" Then for looking: "Glance at the door. Stare at the door." Ask: "When would you use this word and not the plain one?"
note.watch: Ask a child to use two words from one group in two sentences that show the difference. Note the words nobody could act out; teach those before the page is corrected.

lessons.title: The person word: bake, baker
lessons.objective: Children make the word for a person from a verb with the ending -er, as in bake and baker, and say what the new word means.

paper.title: Who Does It? The Person Word

screen.title: Marigold's Knowing Machine — Prefixes & Suffixes Word Meaning

exit.title: Who Does It? The Person Word

note.mistake: Children add -er without the spelling change: "runer," "bakeer," "swimer." They also take every word that ends in -er for a person word, such as "water" and "finger."
note.words: Say: "A baker is a person who bakes. A runner is a person who runs." Give the two spelling moves: "Bake ends in e: drop the e, then add -er. Baker. Run has one short vowel and one consonant at the end: double the consonant, then add -er. Runner." Test a word: "Is a finger a person who fings?"
note.watch: Have the child say the meaning as "a person who…" for each new word. Check the doubled letters (runner, swimmer) and the dropped e (baker, writer); those are the two places where errors gather.

lessons.title: Choose the right form of the word
lessons.objective: Children choose among four words from one family, such as bake, baker, baking, and baked, the one that fits each sentence.

screen.title: Sage's Root Garden — Find the Root Word Family

note.mistake: Children put the words into the blanks in the order they are printed. They choose by meaning alone, which all four words share, and do not listen for what the sentence needs: a person, an action now, or an action that is over.
note.words: Ask what the blank needs: "Is it a person? Something that is happening, after is or are? Something that already happened? Or the plain word, after to, will, or can?" Read the sentence aloud with each word: "Yesterday she… bake? baker? baked. Which one sounds right?" Cross off each word as it is used.
note.watch: Have the child read all four finished sentences aloud. One wrong word forces a second one, so two sentences will sound wrong together; let the child trade the two words.
